name: Hallstatt
sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.

attributes.attribute: archaeological site near Salzburg in Austria holding a treasure of ancient Celtic artifacts
artifacts dated about 700 to 600 B.C.E. between the Urnfield period and the La Tène culture
finds include bronze and iron weapons, tools, ritual objects, and grave goods
site of an early cultural change from cremation to earth burial and of a great salt-mining region

text: Hallstatt is the name of an archaeological site near Salzburg in Austria. Workers found a great treasure of ancient Celtic artifacts there. The finds date from roughly 700 to 600 B.C.E. They came after the Urnfield period and before the La Tène era. The artifacts include weapons and tools of bronze and iron, as well as ritual objects. People buried the objects with their owners. A change from earlier plain objects suggested a cultural shift. Cremation changed to earth entombment only a few generations earlier. Late Hallstatt bodies were laid on four-wheeled wagons and sealed in tombs of oak covered with earth. Bronze vessels, iron spears, and traces of meat and fowl lay with them. This points to an early Celtic belief that the Otherworld needed grave goods for the soul's comfort. The nearby salt-mining region may explain the wealth. Before refrigeration, salt preserved meat, and the cattle-raising Celts valued it across the long winters. Miners dug buried salt and crushed it for transport.

okr.objective: Document Hallstatt as the type site of the early Celtic Iron Age culture.
